source_document.body:
Credit: mas air
By Ian Putzger Americas correspondent
19 November 2026
Mexican cargo airlines are still facing longer waits for US approval of cross-border charter flights, even after Washington lifted restrictions on passenger services from Mexico City to the US last month.
In October 2025, the US sanctioned Mexican carriers in protest over their government’s decision in 2023 to ban freighters from Mexico City’s Benito Juarez Airport (AICM) and curtail take-off slots at the chronically congested airport, steps Washington deemed a violation of the aviation bilateral agreement between the two countries.
Faced with further sanctions and a possible downgrading of its aviation security rating, the Mexican government returned slots taken from US carriers and agreed to allow freighters to return to AICM when operations were not congested.
Amacargo, the Mexico cargo agents’ organisation, welcomed the US lifting its restrictions, calling it a direct impulse to air cargo to strengthen capacity and connectivity with the US market. It noted that airfreight volumes of electronic components and equipment had risen by 40% this year and expressed hopes for stronger connections to key US markets like Los Angeles, Chicago, New York, and Miami.
However, charters, which account for a significant portion of cross-border airfreight traffic, continue to face extended approval times, confirmed Robert Van De Weg, CEO of Mexican cargo airline mas. He expressed confidence that the Mexican and US governments would “work this out”, adding that “the market is very strong right now”.
Statistics from Mexico’s Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) for the first nine months of the year show 5.5% year-on-year growth in the nation’s air cargo volume, led by Felipe Angeles International Airport (AIFA), the Mexican capital’s designated freighter gateway, which reported an increase of 7.2%, to 313,860 tons.
AICM’s throughput rose 2.3%, to 188,418 tons. Opening it again to freighter operators does not seem likely to spur a surge in tonnage, though. To begin with, AFAC has indicated that windows for freighter operations would be between 11.30pm and 12.30am, and from 5am to 6am.
Moreover, AICM director general Juan José Padilla Olmos told Mexican media in late October that none of the freighter operators now using AIFA had signalled any intention to return to AICM. According to Peter Cerdá, executive director and CEO of the Latin American and Caribbean Air Transport Association, a few cargo carriers are interested in a switch, but the majority like the better infrastructure and ease of obtaining landing slots at AIFA.
Passenger airlines are gearing up for expansion. Delta and joint-venture partner Aeromexico have announced new routes from Mexico City to Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan next June.
Mas is also expanding its network, but not to the US this year. In December, it will launch weekly flights to Edmonton, a service anchored by Fresh Direct Produce, one of Canada’s leading importers of fresh produce. The flight will also carry an array of other commodities, including auto parts, pharmaceuticals, tech products, agricultural equipment, and flowers.
Mr Van De Weg intends to open a second route to the US in 2027, as he expects to add at least one converted A330 freighter to the mas fleet in the coming year.
